ideas.title: Downgauge to 0.6 mm DP780 AHSS, delete a doubler
ideas.technicalDescription: Re-engineer the 0.75 mm CR mild-steel bracket into 0.6 mm DP780 dual-phase steel (Rm ≥ 780 MPa, Rp0.2 ≥ 450 MPa vs ~180 MPa for CR4 mild). The bracket is stiffness- and slam-fatigue-driven (E3, E7), not class-A (E6), so the higher yield strength lets you cut gauge ~20% while raising the elastic limit that governs 'no permanent set' after repeated hood slam. Bending stiffness scales with t³ so a section/rib compensation (deeper draw beads across the 17 bends, E4) recovers local stiffness lost to thinner gauge. DP780 at 1,000 €/t vs CRC 800 €/t is a small unit-price premium but the mass drops from 0.21 kg to ~0.155 kg, net material cost neutral-to-down. Crucially the higher-yield web resists the slam permanent-set failure mode directly, so a separately spot-welded local reinforcement (if present in the assembly) can be deleted. DP780 hot-dip or e-coat compatible (E4). Verify formability of the tightest of the 17 bends: DP780 min bend radius ~2.5t, so radii below ~1.5 mm need relief. Springback compensation on the transfer die addresses dimensional hold within 0.5 mm (E3).
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Same progressive/transfer stamping line and e-coat route (E4) — no new process. Die faces need springback recompensation and higher press tonnage (+15–20%) for DP780 vs mild. Tighter bend radii on the 17 bends may need one extra forming station or radius relief. Wear tooling (nitrided/PVD-coated die steel) recommended for AHSS at 60k/yr over 5 yr. E-coat line unchanged. Spot-weld schedule re-tuned for DP780 (lower weldability window, wider electrode force). Net: existing plant, modest tooling revision.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — gauge/mass down plus possible doubler deletion, small alloy premium
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Material €0.20/part × ~26% mass cut ≈ €0.05; doubler + weld deletion €0.30–0.60/part where present; €1.32 baseline (E14/E15)

ideas.riskNotes: DP780 springback risks the 0.5 mm hinge-alignment tolerance (E3) — mitigate with die compensation and first-article CMM. Reduced spot-weldability (E4) narrows the weld window; validate with peel/chisel tests and adjusted schedules. Thinner web could raise NVH/slam booming — confirm modal shift on rig. Fatigue under repeated slam (E3) must be re-validated at 0.6 mm; DP780's higher endurance limit is favourable. No crash regression expected as latch-path only (E7).

ideas.regulatoryContext: EU ELV 2025 25% recycled-content target favours steel, which retains high recycled fraction and closed-loop recyclability.

ideas.title: Attack 61% material overbuy with tighter nesting and blank redesign
ideas.technicalDescription: The engine reports buy-to-fly of 0.339 kg bought per 0.21 kg shipped — 61% overbuy (E16), meaning ~0.129 kg/part becomes skeleton scrap. On a 17-bend deep-drawn part (E4) much of this is web/flange trim and inter-blank webs. Two concrete moves: (1) re-nest the blank on the coil — rotate/interlock the developed flat pattern and reduce inter-part web to the die's minimum carrier width, and evaluate a two-out mirrored layout so a single stroke shares skeleton between a left/right pair; (2) redesign the blank outline to a developed near-net shape (remove the rectangular envelope habit), moving trim from post-form to progressive-die integrated pierce/trim so scrap is coil-optimised. Even a 61%→40% overbuy takes bought mass from 0.339 to ~0.294 kg, cutting material €0.20 by ~15% and reducing the CRC 800 €/t coil consumption. Because the part is not class-A (E6), cosmetic edge quality on trimmed flanges is a non-issue, giving freedom to place blanks tightly. Sell recovered clean single-grade CRC skeleton back as segregated scrap for a higher rebate than mixed.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Requires nesting software study (AutoForm/Logopress) and a die layout revision — potentially a two-out progressive tool if pairing L/R. Coil width may change, needing decoiler/feed re-set. Trim stations rebalanced. No new process or material; same e-coat. Scrap handling upgraded to segregate single-grade CRC skeleton for higher rebate. One-off die rework and PPAP re-run; ongoing coil-yield gain every stroke.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — direct coil-yield recovery, low technical risk
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Material €0.20/part (E15); overbuy 61%→~40% recovers ~€0.03–0.05/part plus scrap-rebate uplift; ×60,000

ideas.riskNotes: Tighter nesting can reduce carrier-strip stiffness causing feed misregistration — validate strip robustness on the transfer line. Blank-edge relocation must not remove material feeding the deepest of the 17 draws (E4), risking splits/thinning that compromise slam durability (E3). Two-out L/R tooling adds die complexity and single-point-of-failure risk. No NCAP/regulatory exposure as internal non-visible part (E6/E7). Confirm scrap segregation logistics.
ideas.benchmarkReference: unverified: Gestamp/Magna progressive-die nesting programmes routinely lift bracket coil yield 10–20% via two-out mirrored layouts on non-class-A parts

ideas.title: Cut 17 bends to ~10 via VA/VE feature attack
ideas.technicalDescription: Seventeen bends (E4) on a non-class-A slam bracket (E6) is a strong VA/VE signal that form features are carrying low value indices. Many bends on hinge reinforcements exist for legacy packaging, incremental stiffening ribs, or tab attachments that a single deeper draw bead or a repositioned weld flange could replace. Function attack: the part must (a) transfer hinge/slam load to the upper rail (E2), (b) resist permanent set (E3), and (c) hold alignment ±0.5 mm (E3). Map each of the 17 bends to one of these functions; bends serving none are candidates for deletion. Consolidate two shallow stiffening bends into one box-section swage that delivers equal or greater section modulus with fewer forming stations. Replace bent locating tabs with pierced pilot holes + a lanced dimple for weld location. Target ~10 bends. Fewer bends = fewer die stations, less springback stack-up (improving the ±0.5 mm hold, E3), lower forming energy, and reduced work-hardening/thinning that currently drives some of the material overbuy (E16). Tooling €0.66/part (E15) is the single largest cost element — station reduction directly attacks it.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Fewer forming stations shortens the progressive/transfer die, cutting die build and maintenance cost and press cycle time. Springback stack-up across fewer bends is easier to compensate, improving dimensional capability (E3). May allow a smaller press bed. Requires re-simulation (AutoForm) to confirm the consolidated swage meets stiffness and the deeper draws don't split. New tool or major die insert revision; PPAP re-run. Setup cost (€0.07/part, E15) and machine time also reduce.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — attacks the dominant tooling cost element and cycle time
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Tooling €0.66 + setup €0.07 + machine €0.11 = €0.84/part (E15); ~30–40% station reduction on these ≈ €0.25–0.35/part × 60,000

ideas.riskNotes: Feature deletion must be load-path validated — removing a stiffening bend could drop section modulus below the slam-fatigue and no-permanent-set requirement (E3). Consolidated box swage needs modal/stiffness sign-off vs baseline (E2). Deeper single draws risk thinning/splits — verify formability. Weld-location changes must keep spot-weld access to the rail (E4). No crash regression (latch path only, E7). Mitigate with CAE topology study and slam-cycle rig test to 30k cycles before release.
ideas.benchmarkReference: unverified: BMW/Audi bracket rationalisation programmes routinely consolidate stiffening bends into box swages, cutting die stations 30–40% on non-visible reinforcements

ideas.title: Integrate bracket into upper-rail reinforcement — delete a part
ideas.technicalDescription: The bracket exists only to transfer hinge/slam loads INTO the upper rail (E2) and is spot-welded to it (E4). Architecturally, this is a candidate for part-count elimination: absorb the bracket's function into the upper-rail inner reinforcement panel as a formed local feature (embossed hinge boss + reinforcing rib pattern) rather than a discrete added part. The hinge mounting holes and slam load path become stamped features of the rail reinforcement, sized in DP780/DP980 locally via a partial patchwork (tailor-welded or spot-welded doubler only where the hinge bolt loads concentrate). This deletes one part number, its dedicated tooling (€0.66/part, E15 — the largest cost driver), its e-coat handling, its logistics, and the spot-weld operation joining it (E4). Because the part is not class-A (E6) and is stiffness/latch-path only (E7), integration doesn't compromise cosmetic or primary-crash requirements. The ±0.5 mm hinge-alignment hold (E3) actually improves when the hinge datum is stamped directly into the rail rather than stacked through a welded bracket's tolerance chain. This is the Tesla/Ford part-consolidation principle applied at the closure-frame level.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Eliminates a standalone stamping, its die, its e-coat pass, its spot-weld fixture and one BOM line. The upper-rail reinforcement tool grows in complexity (added embossments, local patch) and needs re-tuned draw/springback control. Assembly line loses one weld-and-load station. Requires body-shop geometry and welding fixture revision — a larger engineering effort than a part-only change, so best timed to a body refresh or new tool cut. Net structural mass roughly neutral; system part count −1.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — deletes an entire part, its tool and its assembly ops
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Removes most of €1.32/part (E14) net of added rail-tool complexity; conservative €0.80–1.10/part net × 60,000

ideas.riskNotes: Highest engineering risk: re-homologates the closure load path (E2) and the slam-fatigue/no-permanent-set requirement (E3) at the rail level; needs full CAE + rig sign-off. Local hinge-boss stamping in the rail reinforcement must reach the ±0.5 mm tolerance (E3) after body-shop stack-up. Requires body-in-white change control — realistically only at a platform/refresh gate. Spot-weld access and repairability of an integrated boss must be assured. No NCAP regression as latch path only (E7), but hood-slam durability is a warranty-sensitive customer-touch feature.

ideas.title: Commonise as symmetric L/R and carry over across platform
ideas.technicalDescription: Hood hinge brackets are typically handed (left/right) with two mirror part numbers, two tools, two sets of PPAP and inventory. For a stiffness/slam bracket that is non-class-A (E6) and load-path-only (E7), a symmetric ambidextrous design — where the hinge and rail interface features are placed on a mirror-plane so one part serves both sides — collapses two part numbers into one. This doubles the tool's amortisation base (halving effective tooling €0.66/part, E15, the biggest cost element) and halves setup (€0.07/part) and inventory carrying. Extend the same design to carry-over across the OEM's C-segment SUV family and adjacent B/D-segment closures that share hood-slam load magnitudes: a single common hinge-reinforcement geometry qualified once and reused, amortising one tool over multiple programmes rather than 60,000/yr on one. Because the function is generic (transfer hinge/slam load into rail, hold ±0.5 mm — E2/E3), the interface can be standardised. Design the part around a common hinge bolt pattern and a family of rail-flange spacers to absorb the small architectural differences between vehicles, keeping the load-bearing core identical.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: One tool instead of two (or N) — major tooling amortisation gain. Single PPAP, single supplier PO, one inventory SKU, simplified sequencing at body shop. A symmetric part needs a mirror-neutral feature layout that may add a locating feature or two, marginally more forming complexity, but eliminates a whole second die. Carry-over requires cross-programme release governance and a common interface spec. No new process or material; runs on existing stamping + e-coat line (E4).

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — tool and SKU count halved or better, strong amortisation
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Tooling €0.66 + setup €0.07 = €0.73/part (E15); L/R merge + platform reuse cuts effective amortised tool ~30–45% ≈ €0.22–0.33/part × 60,000

ideas.riskNotes: A symmetric design may be slightly heavier or carry redundant features to serve both hands — verify it still meets slam-fatigue/no-permanent-set (E3) on the more highly loaded side. Carry-over across platforms risks over-engineering for lighter programmes and under-engineering for heavier hood variants — bound by worst-case load envelope. Interface standardisation needs cross-programme sign-off, a governance not technical risk. No NCAP/regulatory exposure (non-class-A, latch path only — E6/E7). Mitigate with a design-for-family load study.
ideas.benchmarkReference: unverified: VW MQB and BMW CLAR platforms commonise closure hinge reinforcements across multiple models; symmetric ambidextrous brackets standard in Magna closure kits

ideas.title: Right-size corrosion spec: swap standalone e-coat for lower-cost coating
ideas.technicalDescription: The bracket is fully e-coated as a standalone part (E4), then sits in an under-hood splash-corrosion, 110 °C environment (E5), non-visible (E6). Standalone e-coat (KTL) on a small 0.21 kg bracket is disproportionately expensive per part (finishing €0.01 in-engine but real full-line KTL rack/dip cost is higher off-model). VA/VE the coating spec: (1) if the bracket is spot-welded to the rail before BIW e-coat, it can ride the body's cathodic e-coat pass and the dedicated part-level e-coat is redundant — delete it entirely. (2) Where it must be pre-coated (welded after BIW dip), substitute a zinc-rich pre-primed / GA (galvannealed) or electro-galvanised CRC coil (Z100/ZE) that delivers the required under-hood splash-corrosion life (E5) without a separate KTL pass — coating is applied at the mill on coil, not per-part. Because there is no class-A requirement (E6), cosmetic coating uniformity is irrelevant; only functional red-rust protection matters. Confirm 110 °C service (E5) — galvanneal and cathodic e-coat both tolerate this easily. REACH/ELV compliance: ensure Cr(VI)-free passivation. This removes a whole finishing operation or converts it to a coil-integrated coating with better cut-edge protection at the trimmed flanges.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Option 1 deletes a standalone e-coat/handling step — fewer racks, less WIP, no separate coating logistics. Option 2 moves corrosion protection upstream to pre-coated coil (galvannealed/EG), so stamping runs coated stock and post-coat is unnecessary; requires die adjustment for coated-strip galling and re-tuned weld schedules (zinc coatings affect spot-weld nugget). Both remove or simplify the finishing line for this part. Coil coating adds a small €/t premium but removes per-part coating labour and rework.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — removes or upstreams a finishing operation
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Finishing €0.01 in-engine understates real KTL rack cost; deleting standalone coating + handling ≈ €0.10–0.25/part real; ×60,000

ideas.riskNotes: Must guarantee under-hood splash + 110 °C corrosion durability (E5) — galvanneal/EG cut-edge and weld-zone protection needs salt-spray/CCT validation to programme corrosion spec. If riding BIW e-coat, ensure no faying-surface crevice corrosion at the spot-weld to the rail — apply weld-through sealer. Coated-coil stamping raises die wear and galling; mitigate with tool coatings and lubrication. REACH/ELV: use Cr(VI)-free, cadmium-free passivation. No NCAP impact (E6/E7).
ideas.benchmarkReference: unverified: Most OEM under-hood brackets ride BIW cathodic e-coat or use galvannealed coil (Z/ZE) rather than standalone KTL; PSA/Stellantis GA coil standard for non-visible closures
ideas.regulatoryContext: REACH/ELV 2025 restricts Cr(VI) and cadmium — Cr(VI)-free galvanneal/EG passivation ensures compliance while removing a coating step.

ideas.title: Dual-source to lower-cost footprint with landed-cost discipline
ideas.technicalDescription: The entitlement waterfall shows a footprint premium: the cheapest modelled region for this stamping is Mexico ex-works, releasing €0.10/part (W4), and the engine is uncalibrated with no quotes yet in-corpus (E17), meaning the current price may not be market-tested. As a simple non-visible slam bracket (E6/E7) with no exotic process, this part is an ideal candidate for competitive re-sourcing and dual-sourcing. Concrete levers: (1) RFQ to Czech/Slovak stampers (labour £13–17/hr vs German £38–47/hr) which are logistically close to a German plant — capturing most of the labour arbitrage without the transatlantic supply-chain risk that W4 explicitly excludes; (2) run a should-cost-anchored negotiation using the €1.22 entitlement as the direction indicator (W5), pressing the incumbent on the €0.14 SGA+profit and €0.06 commercial lines (E15); (3) qualify a second source to break single-supplier pricing power over the 5-year programme. Note W4's Mexico number excludes logistics/duty from a German plant — for a 0.21 kg part shipped to Germany, near-shore Czech/Slovak sourcing likely beats Mexico on landed cost despite a higher ex-works rate. Labour is only €0.03/part (E15) so the real prize is tooling amortisation and commercial margin, not labour.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: No design or process change — pure commercial/sourcing action. Requires re-PPAP at the new source, tool transfer or a duplicate tool (capex), and logistics network setup. Near-shore Czech/Slovak sourcing keeps JIT feasibility to a German plant with 1–2 day transit vs weeks from Mexico. Dual-sourcing needs two qualified tools/lines, raising tooling capex but de-risking supply and enabling price competition across the 5-year run.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — labour arbitrage modest (€0.03/part) but commercial/margin leverage material given uncalibrated pricing
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Footprint release €0.10/part (W4) + commercial/SGA pressure on €0.20/part (E15) via competitive RFQ; realistic €0.10–0.18/part × 60,000, net of logistics

ideas.riskNotes: W4's Mexico figure explicitly excludes logistics, duty and supply-chain risk (W4) — a naïve chase of ex-works price can lose the saving to freight and inventory for a light 0.21 kg part; use full landed-cost, favour near-shore. Tool transfer risks dimensional drift on the ±0.5 mm hinge tolerance (E3) — re-PPAP and CMM at new source. Second-source qualification adds lead time. No NCAP/regulatory exposure (E6/E7). Engine uncalibrated (E17) so treat €-figures as directional (W5).

ideas.title: Emerging: laser-cut + fold prototype route, fineblank for scale trim
ideas.technicalDescription: Two emerging/alternative process levers attack the tooling €0.66/part (E15, the dominant cost) and the 61% overbuy (E16). (A) For early production, model-year changes, or the second-source ramp, laser blank-cutting + press-brake / robotic folding of the developed pattern eliminates hard-tool amortisation entirely — the Tesla battery cell-retainer principle of laser-cutting mild steel strip instead of a dedicated stamp. At 60,000/yr this is borderline vs progressive stamping, but for the launch phase and any late design changes it removes tool sunk cost and springback re-cutting risk, and laser trim achieves near-net blanks that slash the 61% overbuy (E16) to near zero. (B) For steady-state volume, fine-blanking the flat features and critical trimmed edges produces net-shape flanges with cut-face quality that eliminates secondary trim/deburr and tightens the ±0.5 mm tolerance chain (E3) — fineblanked edges are dimensionally superior. Because the part is non-class-A (E6) and stiffness-driven (E7), neither route compromises function. A hybrid — fineblank the planar load-bearing feature, form the bends conventionally — can combine net-shape yield with formed stiffness. Evaluate both against the progressive-stamping baseline with the uncalibrated engine (E17) as first data point.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Route A (laser+fold): removes hard tooling — huge capex avoidance for launch/low-rate/second-source; higher per-part cycle time and labour, so suits <30k/yr tranches and change-heavy phases. Near-net laser trim eliminates skeleton scrap (E16). Route B (fineblank): needs a fineblank press and dedicated tool but yields net-shape edges, removing deburr/secondary-trim ops and improving dimensional capability (E3). Both are proven, low-novelty-risk processes. Hybrid needs process split engineering. E-coat/weld routes unchanged (E4).

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — tooling avoidance in launch/low-rate phases and scrap elimination; volume-dependent
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Laser route avoids share of tooling €0.66/part (E15) in launch/change tranches + kills 61% overbuy (E16) recovering ~€0.05/part material; fineblank removes deburr labour

ideas.riskNotes: Laser+fold cycle time may not meet 60k/yr steady-state economically — best as launch/low-rate/second-source and change-management route, not full-volume replacement. Fineblank tool capex is high; payback needs the full 5-yr volume. Fineblanking suits planar features — the 17 bends (E4) still need conventional forming, so a hybrid split adds an operation. Validate laser-cut edge fatigue (HAZ) against slam durability (E3). No NCAP/regulatory risk (E6/E7). Engine uncalibrated (E17) — treat cost crossover point as directional.

ideas.title: DP780 AHSS gauge reduction from 0.75mm mild to 0.55mm
ideas.technicalDescription: Substitute the 0.75mm CR mild steel (Rp0.2 ≈ 180MPa) with 0.55mm DP780 dual-phase (Rp0.2 ≈ 480MPa, Rm ≈ 780MPa). The bracket is stiffness/slam-driven (E3, E7) and not class-A (E6), so surface appearance is irrelevant and the failure mode is permanent set under repeated slam. Yield strength scales roughly 2.6x, allowing ~27% gauge reduction while retaining anti-set margin; bending stiffness (t³) drops, so the 17 bends (E4) must be re-engineered with added flange returns/ribs to recover section modulus in the hinge load path. Slam is a low-cycle fatigue/set problem — DP780's higher yield delays plastic set, which is the governing requirement (E3). DP780 at 1,000 €/t vs CRC 800 €/t: the €/t premium is offset by 27% less mass. Mass drops from 0.21kg to ~0.153kg. Material cost (E15: €0.20) falls with net mass; the buy-to-fly 61% overbuy (E16) also shrinks proportionally. DP780 is fully spot-weldable (E4) and e-coat compatible (E4).
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Existing progressive/transfer die must be re-cut for thinner stock and revised bend geometry to recover stiffness; springback compensation increases with DP780 so die tryout and CAE-based springback prediction are required. Spot-weld schedules re-qualified (higher strength, narrower weld window). No new press class needed — same tonnage envelope. 17 bends retained but some converted to stiffening beads. E-coat line unchanged. Coil sourcing shifts to AHSS supplier but DP780 is a mainstream grade with broad availability in Germany (Salzgitter, TKS).

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — small absolute part but material + mass both fall
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: 0.057kg mass-out × 60k × net €/kg delta (DP780 premium partly offsets); material €0.20→~€0.16

ideas.riskNotes: Springback on 17 bends in higher-strength steel risks hinge alignment drift beyond 0.5mm (E3) — mitigate with die compensation and post-form gauging. Reduced t³ stiffness could raise NVH/slam resonance; recover with beads. DP780 formability lower — check for edge cracking at pierced holes. Weld-window narrowing risks cold welds; re-qualify RSW schedule. E-coat throw unaffected.

ideas.title: HSLA S420 as low-cost strength upgrade over mild CR
ideas.technicalDescription: If DP780 forming risk is unacceptable on 17 tight bends (E4), the intermediate lever is HSLA S420 (microalloyed, Rp0.2 ≈ 420MPa, Rm ≈ 480MPa) at 830 €/t — only marginally above CRC 800 €/t but with 2.3x the yield of mild steel. Because slam resistance is a permanent-set (yield-governed) problem (E3), S420 lets the bracket hold hinge alignment with better anti-set margin at the SAME 0.75mm gauge, OR a modest downgauge to ~0.62mm. HSLA has far better formability than DP780 (higher n-value at these strengths, no martensite islands to crack at bend radii), so the 17 bends survive with minimal springback rework — decisive for a stiffness-driven bracket that is not class-A (E6). Spot-weldable and e-coat compatible (E4). This is the pragmatic 'first step' substitution: near-zero material €/t penalty, meaningful mass-out if downgauged, low forming risk. Buy-to-fly overbuy (E16, 61%) reduces with any downgauge.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Minimal die change if gauge held at 0.75mm — only a grade swap in the coil spec and re-tryout for the slightly higher springback. If downgauged to 0.62mm, die re-cut and springback compensation needed but far less severe than DP780. Spot-weld schedule re-qualified (modest). Same press, same e-coat line. HSLA S420 widely stocked in Germany — no supply risk. Lower scrap/crack rate than AHSS route.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low-Medium — small part, but very low implementation risk

ideas.riskNotes: At held gauge, no mass benefit — value is only realised via downgauge, which reduces stiffness (t³) and risks slam resonance/set (E3); recover with beads. Springback slightly higher than mild — re-tryout. Edge quality at pierced holes better than DP but check hole expansion. Low regulatory/NCAP risk as bracket is only a hood-latch load path element (E7).
ideas.benchmarkReference: unverified: VW MQB uses HSLA S420 microalloyed grades broadly for non-class-A closure reinforcements (2020+)

ideas.title: Blank nesting redesign to cut 61% material overbuy
ideas.technicalDescription: The engine reports a buy-to-fly of 0.339kg bought per 0.21kg shipped — a 61% material overbuy (E16). For a stamped bracket this is dominated by blank skeleton/web scrap around the developed flat pattern of a 17-bend part (E4). Attack it three ways: (1) re-nest the developed blank on the coil with tighter part-to-part webs and shared-edge nesting (two mirrored brackets nested head-to-tail); (2) narrow coil width selection to match the developed pattern envelope, eliminating side-trim scrap; (3) convert to a progressive-die layout with carrier-strip optimisation and add-on scrap-chopper to enable a denser strip. Because the part is not class-A (E6) and only moderately loaded (E7), no cosmetic edge constraints limit nesting. Reducing overbuy from 61% toward a realistic 25–30% for a multi-bend part recovers material (E15: €0.20) and reduces coil purchase — the single largest controllable variable-cost lever here since tooling (€0.66) is fixed sunk. Every kg of skeleton scrap sells back only at scrap price (~10–15% of CRC), so gross recovery is nearly the full coil €/t.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Requires a new strip-layout study and possibly a re-cut progressive die or added stations for pilot/carrier optimisation. If a mirrored two-out nest is adopted, die complexity and press tonnage rise but per-part material falls sharply. Scrap handling (chopper, conveyor) added. Coil width change requires supplier re-slit spec. No change to bends, welds, e-coat. Nesting CAE (AutoForm/logopress) validates the developed pattern before die commitment.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — directly targets the 61% overbuy, the biggest variable lever
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Cut overbuy 61%→28% ≈ 0.08kg bought/part saved × 60k × ~€0.80/kg CRC net of scrap credit

ideas.riskNotes: Tighter webs risk blank distortion, burr, and feed instability; validate with die trials. Two-out mirrored nest raises tooling cost — payback depends on 5-yr programme (300k units) amortisation. Coil re-slit narrows supplier flexibility. No functional/NCAP risk since geometry and material unchanged (E7). Scrap-price volatility affects recovery value.
ideas.benchmarkReference: unverified: Gestamp closure-reinforcement nesting programmes routinely cut buy-to-fly from 60%+ to <30% via two-out layouts (industry standard)
ideas.regulatoryContext: Reduced scrap supports EU ELV 2025 material-efficiency intent.

ideas.title: Relocate stamping to lower-cost footprint with logistics offset
ideas.technicalDescription: The entitlement waterfall (W4) shows the cheapest modelled region for Stamping/Deep Drawing is Mexico, releasing €0.10/part ex-works (€1.32→€1.22). Germany labour is €38–47/hr; Mexico €6.8–10/hr. For a low-value, tooling-heavy bracket the labour+overhead delta (E15: labour €0.03, overhead €0.04, setup €0.07) is modest per part, so the honest lever is transferring the die to an existing lower-cost stamping supplier that already produces for this OEM in a low-labour region — but the part's small size and low value means logistics/duty/inventory (explicitly NOT in W4) can easily erase the €0.10. The defensible move is to source from a Czech/Slovak stamping supplier (€13–17/hr) already inside the EU customs union and near the German assembly plant, capturing part of the labour delta WITHOUT trans-Atlantic freight, duty, or 6-week pipeline inventory on a slam-critical alignment part (E3). This is a commercial/footprint lever, not a design change.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Die transferred or duplicated at the receiving plant; requires PPAP re-run, weld/e-coat re-qualification at new site, and logistics setup. No product change. Small bracket ships densely (high parts/container), so freight per part is low intra-EU. Dual-sourcing risk during transfer managed with safety stock.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low — €0.10/part ceiling, partly eaten by logistics
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: €0.10/part ex-works (W4) × 60k, less realistic intra-EU freight; Czech route captures ~€0.06 net

ideas.riskNotes: Trans-Atlantic (Mexico) route adds duty, 6-week pipeline and supply risk on a 0.5mm-alignment-critical part (E3) — intra-EU (Czech/Slovak) route preferred to avoid these. PPAP and re-qualification cost may exceed 1-yr saving — check against 5-yr programme. Tooling transfer risks die damage. No NCAP/regulatory change.
ideas.benchmarkReference: German OEMs routinely dual-source low-value closure brackets from Czech/Slovak stampers (€13–17/hr) to capture labour delta without duty (2023)

ideas.title: Commonise left/right and cross-platform bracket variants
ideas.technicalDescription: A hood hinge reinforcement is typically handed (LH/RH) and often near-identical across platform derivatives. Because the part is not class-A (E6) and its function is purely load transfer into the rail (E2, E7), the geometric constraints are structural, not styling-driven — which makes commonisation far easier than for visible parts. Two moves: (1) design a single symmetric bracket usable on both LH and RH hinge positions via a mirror-tolerant 17-bend pattern (E4), halving the number of unique part numbers and dies; (2) carry the SAME bracket across the C-segment SUV's platform siblings (other closures/derivatives sharing the upper-rail interface). Consolidating part numbers spreads the €0.66 tooling (E15) — the dominant cost line — across 2–4x the volume, and cuts PPAP, inventory, and logistics SKUs. At 60,000/yr per programme, doubling effective volume roughly halves per-part tooling amortisation. This is a pure commonisation lever requiring no material or process change and thus no functional risk to the slam duty (E3).
ideas.manufacturingImpact: One die replaces two (LH/RH) if symmetry achieved; die amortised over combined volume. Requires the hinge interface on both sides to accept a common part — packaging negotiation with rail and hinge teams. If cross-platform, part released against multiple BOMs; supplier runs longer batches, lowering setup (E15: €0.07) per part. No change to forming, welding, e-coat. Inventory and PPAP SKUs reduced.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High — tooling is the dominant cost line and it is halved
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: €0.66 tooling/part halved via 2x effective volume amortisation × 60k, plus setup and SKU reduction

ideas.riskNotes: Symmetric design may compromise optimal hinge geometry on one side — validate slam alignment (E3) on both. Cross-platform carry-over locks the part against multiple programme timings; a change on one platform forces re-validation on all. Requires cross-programme governance. No NCAP/material risk. Risk of over-design if the common part must satisfy the worst-case load of all applications.

ideas.title: Roll-forming for repetitive bend profile at 300k lifetime volume
ideas.technicalDescription: The bracket has 17 bends (E4) and is not class-A (E6). If a meaningful subset of those bends form a constant cross-section along one axis, roll-forming can replace part of the deep-draw stamping route. Roll-forming produces long profiles with many bends at very low per-part material scrap and modest tooling relative to a multi-station progressive die — directly attacking both the €0.66 tooling line and the 61% buy-to-fly overbuy (E15, E16), since roll-forming has near-net edge utilisation with no skeleton web scrap. At 60,000/yr over 5 years (300,000 lifetime), the roll-form line's tooling amortises well. The developed part is then cut-to-length and secondary-formed for the non-constant hinge features. Roll-forming also work-hardens the section, raising anti-set resistance for slam duty (E3) at the same or lower gauge. Spot-weldable and e-coat compatible (E4). This is an emerging/underused process lever for multi-bend brackets that the deterministic engine excluded (W3 notes 14 routes excluded on DFM score) — worth a targeted DFM re-score.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Roll-form line (sequential roller stands) replaces the transfer/progressive die for the constant-section portion; a short secondary press operation adds the hinge-specific 3D features. Dramatically lower material scrap (no skeleton). Roller tooling cheaper to modify than a full progressive die. Cut-to-length and pierce integrated inline. E-coat and weld unchanged. Requires the part to have enough constant-section content to justify the line — geometry-dependent (no 3D model supplied, E8).

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — strong if constant-section content is high
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Near-zero skeleton scrap cuts 61% overbuy (E16); roller tooling amortised over 300k lifetime vs €0.66 progressive die

ideas.riskNotes: Only viable if the 17 bends include substantial constant-section geometry — unverified without a 3D model (E8); requires geometry review first. Roll-form end-flare and cut-off burr must be controlled near the hinge datum (0.5mm, E3). Secondary op adds a station. Work-hardening may reduce weld ductility — re-qualify RSW. Process-change gate per W3.
ideas.benchmarkReference: Roll-formed door-frame and closure reinforcements at Shape Corp / voestalpine achieve <10% scrap vs 40–60% stamping (2023)
ideas.regulatoryContext: Lower scrap supports EU ELV 2025 material-efficiency targets.

ideas.title: Topology-driven lightening holes and rib beads to mass-out
ideas.technicalDescription: The design is stiffness-driven and not class-A (E6, E7), which is exactly the case where topology optimisation removes non-load-bearing material. Run a stiffness/slam-load topology study on the bracket to (1) punch lightening holes in low-stress regions between the hinge bolt pattern and the weld flange, and (2) add embossed stiffening beads that recover section modulus so gauge/mass can drop without losing anti-set performance (E3). Because slam is a set/stiffness problem, moving material to where the bending moment is highest and voiding it elsewhere is directly effective. Lightening holes also reduce blank area, improving buy-to-fly (E16) and cutting material (E15: €0.20). The 17 existing bends (E4) already provide some stiffening; topology tells us which are redundant and where beads replace bends, potentially reducing bend count (fewer die stations, lower tooling). Piercing holes in a progressive die is nearly free per part. This mass-out is achievable at constant material grade, so it stacks with the HSLA/DP substitution ideas rather than competing with them.
ideas.manufacturingImpact: Progressive die gains pierce/emboss stations for holes and beads; net die complexity may fall if beads let you delete redundant bends. Blank area reduced → less coil consumed. Springback re-tuned for new bead pattern. No new equipment. Spot-weld flange preserved. E-coat drainage actually improves with lightening holes (relevant to E5 splash-corrosion environment — avoids water traps). CAE topology + slam-durability sign-off required before die commit.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium — mass-out plus possible bend/station reduction

ideas.riskNotes: Lightening holes near the hinge load path risk stress concentration and premature set under repeated slam (E3) — hole placement must be CAE-verified in low-stress zones only. Beads change resonance; check NVH. Reducing material could drop stiffness below the 0.5mm alignment threshold — validate. E-coat coverage at hole edges must be confirmed for the 110°C splash-corrosion duty (E5). No NCAP risk (E7).

ideas.regulatoryContext: Lightweighting supports EU ELV 2025 and fleet CO2 compliance.
